old: Once, its two halves named a drinking vessel and a flat plank, joined into one household word.
Literally a plank meant to hold cups, before it grew doors and became something to shut.
Say 'cup' and 'board' quickly enough, and centuries of sound-shift do the rest.
clues: This piece of household storage furniture began, centuries ago, as nothing more than a simple shelf for holding drinking vessels.
In British homes it is the everyday name for a kitchen cabinet: a shelved space behind a door for mugs, plates and tins, smaller than a walk-in pantry.
Old Mother Hubbard went to hers to fetch her poor dog a bone and found it bare. Brits also hide skeletons in one rather than a closet.
